notes.meaning: Martha had whispered to Mary that Jesus was asking for her. Mary jumped up at once and hurried to Him. Matthew Henry pictures her running for joy, not stopping for the usual customs of mourning. She did not even ask her guests' leave before going.

Jesus had stayed outside the village, where Martha had met Him. Burial places were outside towns, so He was probably near the tomb. Matthew Henry says He stayed close to the work He had come to do. He also did not want to draw a crowd into town. Another suggestion is that He wanted to meet the sisters away from the crowd of mourners.

The friends comforting Mary had not heard Martha call her. They thought she was going to weep at the grave, so they followed her. They meant well. But God used their mistake to bring many witnesses to the miracle that was about to happen.

Mary fell at Jesus' feet, something Martha had not done. This was the same Mary who once sat at His feet to learn from Him. Now she came there in her trouble, honouring Him as more than a man. She said almost exactly what Martha had said. The sisters had probably said it to each other many times. Calvin notes a weakness in her words, because Jesus' power was not limited to being in the room.

Jesus saw Mary and the mourners crying, and He was deeply stirred inside. He shared fully in human feelings, but without sin. Calvin says He felt our troubles as if they were His own. He was also moved by the misery of the whole human race, which He came to rescue. 'Spirit' here means Jesus' own inner self.

differ.view: The word is close to anger. Jesus was outraged at death, humanity's great enemy, and at the damage sin has done.
Jesus' groaning was His way of holding back tears. His feelings were not passions that swept Him away. He chose them, and they were fully in His control.

notes.meaning: Jesus asked where Lazarus was buried. He could have known, but He spoke as an ordinary man would and let them lead the way. Matthew Henry adds that this kept anyone from suspecting a trick planned between Him and Lazarus. It also shows His care for the bodies of His people in the grave.

This is the shortest verse in the Bible, but it says a great deal. Jesus shed quiet tears, not the loud wailing of the mourners. It shows He was truly human and a tender friend. It also shows that grieving when someone dies is not wrong, even for people who hope in the resurrection.

differ.view: Jesus was about to raise Lazarus, so He was not crying over Lazarus' death. His tears were sorrow over sin and all the harm it brings.

notes.meaning: Some onlookers saw His tears as a sign of how much He loved Lazarus. Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke note that we have even more reason to say this. Jesus did not just cry for us; He gave His life for us.

Others hinted that Jesus' power had limits. They suggested that if He could not keep His friend alive, perhaps He had not really healed the blind man either. Wesley calls this a strange mix of faith and unbelief, because they never imagined He could raise Lazarus. Jesus soon answered them by doing something greater.

Once more deeply moved, Jesus came to the tomb. Calvin pictures Him as a champion getting ready to fight death itself. The tomb was a cave closed with a large stone. This was a common kind of burial, like the cave where Abraham's family was buried.

Jesus had others do what human hands could do: move the stone. He kept for Himself only what no person could do. Martha protested that after four days the body would smell. In her, faith and reason were struggling, and her hope dimmed for a moment. Her words also proved that Lazarus was really dead, so no one could call it a trick.

Jesus gently corrected Martha by reminding her of His promise. The 'glory of God' means God's power and goodness, shown here in raising Lazarus. This was the purpose of the miracle, as Jesus said at the start of the chapter. If we trust Christ's word, we will see God's glory.

Jesus looked up and thanked His Father, even before Lazarus came out. He was sure He would be heard, because the Father always hears Him. He prayed out loud for the people's sake, so they would believe God had sent Him. It also showed He was not using evil powers or magic. Matthew Henry says this teaches us to call God 'Father' and to give thanks when we pray.

differ.view: Jesus had already prayed, likely during His groaning, and here He thanks the Father for the answer. In this He shows Himself as the Father's servant.
Jesus was not asking His Father for help. He acted as Lord of life and death, and thanked the Father for this chance to show His power and God's praise.

notes.meaning: Jesus shouted, 'Lazarus, come out!' He spoke openly so everyone could hear, unlike magicians who whispered. Only His word was used, which shows His own divine power. Matthew Henry sees it as a picture of the gospel calling spiritually dead people to life. It is also a picture of the last day, when Christ's voice will raise all the dead.

Lazarus came out still wrapped in his burial cloths, so all could see it was really him. He came back not just to life but to health. Jesus told the bystanders to unwrap him, so their own hands could witness the miracle. Lazarus came back to this earthly life and would one day die again.

Many who had come to comfort Mary saw it with their own eyes and believed in Jesus. In this, God's Son was glorified, just as Jesus had said. Adam Clarke notes that their kind visit to grieving friends became the way they came to faith.

Others saw the same miracle but went to tell Jesus' enemies. The same evidence softened some hearts and hardened others. Wesley links this to Jesus' warning that some will not believe even if someone rises from the dead.

The leaders called the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council. They admitted Jesus was doing many miracles. They feared everyone would follow Him and Rome would destroy their 'place', meaning the temple, and their nation. Wesley says the right answer to 'What are we to do?' was simply to believe. Sadly, by rejecting Jesus, they brought on the very ruin they feared.

Caiaphas was high priest 'that year', the year Christ died. The office was meant to last for life, but the Romans changed high priests whenever they liked. He rudely brushed off the council's slow debate. He said it was better for one man to die than for the whole nation to be lost. It was clever thinking but not right thinking. We must not do evil so that good may come.

John explains that God guided Caiaphas' words beyond what he meant. As high priest, he unknowingly foretold that Jesus would die for the nation. Christ would die in the people's place. Caiaphas was not a true prophet. God used a wicked man's mouth to state a precious truth, and speaking such words is no proof of a godly heart.

Jesus would die not only for the Jewish nation. He would also die for God's children scattered everywhere, to gather them into one family. This echoes His words in John 10 about 'other sheep' and one flock. His death draws people to Himself and joins them to one another.

differ.view: They are called God's children because God chose them beforehand, even before they hear the gospel and believe.
These are all God's children through all ages and nations, gathered into one Church.

notes.meaning: From that day the council was united in planning to kill Jesus. Caiaphas' advice silenced anyone who disagreed. Their minds were already made up; they only had to work out how. Matthew Henry notes that this makes Jesus' later trial only a show.

Jesus stopped moving about openly. He went with His disciples to Ephraim, a small town near the wilderness, likely north of Jerusalem. He was not running from His calling. He was waiting for the time God had set, at the coming Passover. Barnes notes He never risked His life without need.

The Passover feast was near. Many came to Jerusalem early to go through the washing rites the law required, such as after touching a dead body. Then they would be fit to eat the Passover meal. Matthew Henry draws a lesson: we too should prepare our hearts before we come to meet God.

In the temple, people kept looking for Jesus and wondering if He would dare to come. The leaders had ordered that anyone who knew where He was must report it, as if He were an outlaw. Barnes notes Jesus faced danger on one side and duty on the other, and chose duty. Matthew Henry says that even so, the Lord kept Him hidden until His time came.
